text: Massimo Cacciari (Italian pronunciation: [ˈmassimo katˈtʃaːri]; born 5 June 1944) is an Italian philosopher and politician who served as Mayor of Venice from 1993 to 2000 and from 2005 to 2010. Born in Venice, he graduated in philosophy from the University of Padua in 1967, where he also earned his doctorate, writing a thesis on Immanuel Kant's Critique of Judgment. In 1985, he became professor of Aesthetics at the Architecture Institute of Venice. In 2002, he founded the Department of Philosophy at the University of Vita-Salute San Raffaele in Milan, where he was appointed Dean in 2005. Cacciari has founded several philosophical reviews and published essays centered on the "negative thought" inspired by authors like Friedrich Nietzsche, Martin Heidegger, and Ludwig Wittgenstein. In the 1980s, he worked with the Italian composer Luigi Nono, a political activist whose music opposed bourgeois cultural constructs; Cacciari arranged philosophical lyrics for Nono's works such as Das Atmende Klarsein, Io, and the opera Prometeo. After a brief affiliation with Potere Operaio, a radical left-wing worker's party, Cacciari joined the Italian Communist Party (PCI). In the 1970s, he was responsible for industrial politics for the PCI Veneto section and, in 1976, was elected to the Italian Chamber of Deputies, serving on the Parliamentary commission for industry from 1976 to 1983. After Enrico Berlinguer's death in 1984, Cacciari left the Communist Party and adopted more moderate positions, though he remained within the centre-left coalition. In 1993, he was elected mayor of Venice, a position he held until 2000. He was also considered a potential national leader of the coalition, later named The Olive Tree, but his defeat in the 2000 election as governor of the Veneto region diminished this prospect. In a surprise move in 2005, Cacciari ran again for mayor of Venice and was elected by a slight majority over former magistrate Felice Casson, the magistrate who had previously indicted Cacciari for criminal negligence related to the 1996 fire at Venice's La Fenice opera house; Cacciari was later acquitted of all charges in that case. The volumes Icone della Legge (Icons of the Law) and The Necessary Angel (1986) include only a few pages on the philosophy of the icon and the thought of the Russian mystic Pavel Aleksandrovič Florensky, with Cacciari asserting that angels in Christianity originate from the angelology of ancient Babylonia. Emanuele Severino, Gianni Vattimo, Massimo Cacciari, and Umberto Galimberti have been described as "neopagan" philosophers insofar as they interpret Christianity as a historically significant but now outdated moment for the West (rather than in the common sense of the term).
